1.pericope_label: The oath at Mizpeh that no man give his daughter to Benjamin

schools.summary: Gill sets the oath in its sequence — the tribes convened at Mizpeh, heard the Levite's account, demanded the men of Gibeah, found the demand refused and war preparing, resolved on destroying Gibeah and every city that had sent men against them, and then bound themselves to treat the survivors as heathens and not intermarry with them.

Henry recovers two acts of zeal not reported earlier: the great execration called the Cherem, devoting to destruction any city that failed to send its quota to the assembly, and this marriage oath, which he insists bound only the thousands then present and not their posterity, and was framed with no design to extirpate the tribe but to treat the actual perpetrators like the devoted nations of Canaan, whom Israel was forbidden both to spare and to marry. He observes that the Levite's sending the mangled pieces of his wife's body round the tribes inflamed them more than any narrative could, so much does the eye affect the heart. On the outcome he judges as Keil does: they repented for Benjamin their brother, not of their zeal against the sin but of carrying the matter further than was just, and from that he draws four maxims — that there may be over-doing in well-doing, and no divinity is good that swallows up humanity; that even necessary justice should be done with compassion; that strong passions make work for repentance; and that a civil war admits no triumph, since whichever side wins the community loses.

Clarke notes that this oath had not been mentioned before, and reads it as evidence that the war began with a settled determination to destroy the Benjamites utterly: if any escaped the sword no man might give him a daughter, so the remnant must soon have been annihilated.

Ellicott marks the same gap in the record and adds from the sequel that this was not merely an oath but a vow under a curse, of the kind taken by the men who bound themselves to kill Paul. Keil weighs outcome against cause: the beginning was sound, the resolution to punish Gibeah with the full severity of the law being urged by the duty to root out the evil, the war justified by the tribe's taking the culprits' side, and approved by the Lord — but after two defeats personal revenge disturbed the righteous cause and carried the warriors into a war of extermination neither commanded by the law nor justified by the circumstances.

debates.question: Was the destruction of Benjamin the intention of the oath, or an excess beyond it?

positions.position: the intention — the war began with a settled purpose to destroy the tribe utterly
an excess — the cause was just and even approved, but revenge after two defeats carried it into a war of extermination

outliers.note: turns the episode into a rule of proportion — there may be over-doing in well-doing, and that is no good divinity which swallows up humanity

themes: an oath the narrative never reported
whether extermination was intended from the first

2.pericope_label: Weeping at the house of God, and the sentence on Jabesh-gilead

schools.summary: Gill dissents on the place, denying that the house of God means Bethel, as the Targum and Septuagint took it, and setting the scene at Shiloh where tabernacle and ark then stood; they came, he says, not to give thanks for the victory but to lament Benjamin's case and take counsel how to repair the loss. He has them rising early after fasting and prayer, hoping the difficulty would be removed in the way of duty, and states the legal mechanism of the remedy: Jabesh-gilead, having stayed away from Mizpeh, had never sworn to withhold their daughters, so wives might be taken thence without breaking any oath.

Clarke reads the Hebrew flatly as Bethel and puts the temper of the weeping shortly — revenge satisfied, reflection brings contrition. He refuses to let the lament pass as a real question, calling why is this come to pass impertinent, since they knew perfectly well how: it was right that Gibeah be punished, but they carried revenge too far. He infers that Benjamin's women and children had all been massacred deliberately, so that any survivor should find neither wife nor daughter, and will not soften the sequel — the crime of Gibeah was of the deepest dye, the punishment ran to a criminal excess taking guilty and innocent together, and the remedy was equally abominable. On the altar he notes that needing to build one shows the place was no regular sanctuary, and the act was not according to law; but there was neither king nor law among them.

Keil agrees on Bethel and reads the altar as a practical expression of their wish, since they knew nothing could succeed without reconciliation to the Lord, while granting there is something strange in erecting one there. Ellicott answers Clarke on the lament: it is no inquiry into a cause too patent to need one, but a wail of regret carrying a prayer to be shown how the calamity might be met, and in the threefold repetition of the name Israel he finds a nation that had not lost its sense of corporate unity — their wild justice mingled with a still wilder mercy. He identifies the spirit of the great oath with the curse on Meroz, and reads the search for defaulters shrewdly, the people being sick with slaughter and inquiring after absentees only to soften their own rash vow. He closes by tracing Jabesh afterwards, whose peril first roused Saul and whose men alone saved the bodies of Saul and Jonathan — proof the town recovered from the extermination inflicted here.

positions.position: Shiloh, where the tabernacle and ark then stood
Bethel, as the Hebrew and the versions read it

debates.question: Is 'why is this come to pass' a real question?

positions.position: no, and an impertinent one — they knew perfectly well how it had come to pass
not an inquiry but a wail of regret, carrying a prayer to be shown a remedy

the oath turned into an expedient against Jabesh-gilead

9.pericope_label: Four hundred virgins of Jabesh, and two hundred still wanting

schools.summary: Gill takes the muster simply as a check on who had come up, particularly whether the men of Jabesh had, an information having been laid. On the force he notes the Vulgate has ten thousand where the Hebrew, Targum, Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic read twelve, Josephus with them, and passes on Bunting's estimate of fifty-two miles from Shiloh. He is candid where others are not about the arithmetic of conscience: how the men of Israel did not think themselves bound by their oath to put the four hundred virgins to death with the rest, he says, is not easy to say — whether necessity was held to excuse it, or they had a dispensation on consulting the Lord. He is equally frank about how they were identified, by age, unmarried state and common report, unless one supposes they were examined by matrons. He has the six hundred returning at once with the messengers, trusting the assurances given them.

Clarke glosses the overture — to call peaceably is to proclaim peace, meaning that the enmity was over and the fugitives might safely leave their stronghold — and counts the shortfall plainly: six hundred men at Rimmon, four hundred women saved, two hundred still wanting.

Ellicott doubts that a second numbering is meant at all, since the absence of one town might have escaped notice in the tally at Mizpeh and it would now be enough to consult the lists already drawn; he takes the twelve thousand as a thousand from each tribe, as in the war against Midian. On the masculine pronoun in they brought them he compares a Greek idiom, admits no other trace of it in Hebrew, and then gives his real reason for referring it to the virgins — we can hardly suppose captives were brought all the way to Shiloh and there killed in cold blood under the ban. On the closing words he is sharpest: the breach was caused by their own headstrong fury, righteous though the original cause had been, yet in the Hebrew conception the results even of man's sin are referred to Jehovah as overruling them, so that it was needless and not quite honest of Jerome to drop the Lord from the Vulgate. Keil states the commission with its limit — every male and every woman who had known man to be banned, which implied that virgins should be spared — and explains that no wives could be found nearer home because out of Benjamin every woman had been destroyed.

debates.question: How could the four hundred virgins be spared consistently with the ban?

positions.position: the instruction itself limited the ban to males and to women who had known man, so virgins were exempt by its own terms
unclear — perhaps necessity was held to excuse it, or a dispensation was obtained; it is not easy to say
the question hardly arises, since we cannot suppose captives were carried to Shiloh only to be killed there in cold blood

outliers.note: charges Jerome with dishonesty for omitting 'the Lord' from the statement that the Lord had made a breach in the tribes

themes: why four hundred were spared from a ban that spared nobody else
the breach, and who is said to have made it

16.pericope_label: Keeping the vow in the letter: the feast at Shiloh

schools.summary: Gill works out the property logic that made the rescue necessary. The inheritance had been divided by lot to Benjamin and belonged to that tribe only; it now devolved of right on the six hundred survivors, whose number must therefore be increased that they might occupy what was theirs and rebuild it.

Henry follows Bishop Patrick in making the feast tabernacles, that being the only season at which Jewish virgins were allowed to dance, and then not for recreation but to express holy joy as David danced before the ark. He insists the dancing was modest — not mixed, no men joining, no married women forgetting their gravity — yet notes it left the dancers easy prey, and quotes Bishop Hall that the ambushes of evil spirits carry many souls from dancing to a fearful desolation. On the expedient itself he is resigned rather than approving: a sorry salvo is better than none to save an oath, but far better to be cautious in vowing, so that there be no need afterwards to say before the angel that it was an error — the less consideration goes into a vow, the more is needed afterwards to keep it.

Clarke will name none of the three feasts, observing only that all fell when the vines were in full leaf, so the Benjaminites could hide there. He can see no reason for the elaborate description of Shiloh's site unless the feast was that year held somewhere unusual, and the Benjaminites, shut up in Rimmon, needed exact directions.

Keil states the elders' principle: Benjamin must survive as a tribe, so its land remains an independent possession, and since the oath barred the other tribes from giving their daughters, hardly any course was left but to let the Benjaminites seize wives themselves. Ellicott renders the clause as a grant rather than a necessity, and finds the repair incomplete — Benjamin never quite recovered, and though it gave Israel the second judge and the first king, it became a satellite of the more powerful Judah. On the vow he is severest of all: they keep it in the letter while breaking it in the spirit, as Themison in Herodotus threw Phronima into the sea and had her drawn out again; the guilt of breaking a guilty vow is only the original guilt of ever having made it, and what they should have done was to pray God to forgive the brutal vehemence that disgraced a righteous cause and let the remnant intermarry again. He judges the description of Shiloh's site a later scribe's gloss, which alone has let us identify the modern Seilun.

debates.question: Why is the site of Shiloh described in such elaborate detail?

positions.position: a later scribe’s marginal gloss, needless to the elders themselves but necessary once Shiloh lay desolate
because the feast was that year held somewhere unusual, and the Benjaminites shut up in Rimmon needed exact directions

outliers.note: reduces the whole casuistry to one sentence — the guilt of breaking a guilty vow is only the original guilt of ever having made it

themes: the letter and the spirit of the ban
which feast, and why the site is described so minutely

21.pericope_label: The dancers seized, and no king in Israel

schools.summary: Gill explains why the daughters of Shiloh were available: only males were obliged to attend the feast, but women might come if they wished, and those of Shiloh, living where the tabernacle stood, always attended with joy and dancing as an expression of religious gladness — dancing by themselves and not with men, which made them the easier to seize. He reads the fathers' expected complaint as a formal action, a demand that the offenders be summoned and tried, or else that war be renewed; and he dates the closing formula precisely, Joshua being dead and no judge yet risen, so that all the matter of these last chapters falls between.

Clarke states the order plainly — let each man seize a woman and from that hour consider her his wife — and then lays three readings of the obscure pacifying verse side by side. The Vulgate makes the elders plead that the Benjaminites asked for wives and were refused, so the fault lies with the fathers, a rendering in which Clarke suspects Jerome had the Sabines in mind; Houbigant has them argue that the Benjaminites took no wives to the war and that refusal now would be the sin; the Authorised text rests the plea on Israel's own failure to spare Benjamin's women. He leaves the reader to choose, allowing the Vulgate a good sense but thinking Houbigant nearest. On the sequel he judges the Benjaminites to have behaved honourably, the women coming to an inheritance at least equal to their own, since six hundred men now shared what had belonged to many thousands. He closes the book with a disclaimer — let no one suppose the writer justifies these atrocities by relating them, and his impartiality in recording what was so much to his country's discredit is itself the strongest proof of authenticity — and sets beside it the Roman parallel of Romulus and the Sabine women.

Ellicott takes the dances for those of the vintage festival, points to a fountain in a narrow dale near Shiloh as probably the scene, and widens the phrase daughters of Shiloh to include the many women employed about the tabernacle and not only worshippers, there having been no regular town there. He renders the elders' plea as present them to us rather than be favourable to them, and thinks the parents the sooner consoled because the land now held by six hundred far exceeded their wants. His closing note is hopeful: the formula is added once more as an apology for the lawless crimes, evaded vows and unhallowed excesses the historian has faithfully narrated, out of which depths the judges partially raised their countrymen until the nation was ripe for monarchy. Keil records the seizure and the rebuilding, and closes on the two final remarks, adding that the writer never says whether the fathers complained because it would have made no difference to the facts.

debates.question: How should the elders' plea to the fathers be read?

positions.position: the Benjamites asked for wives and were refused, so the fault lies with the fathers (Vulgate), or they took no wives to the war and refusal now would be sin (Houbigant) — the latter probably nearest
render it present them to us, or gratify us in them; the drift is a promise to pacify the parents by showing the cherem was not violated
words the elders will speak in the Benjaminites’ name to the complaining relatives

outliers.note: insists that relating an atrocity is not justifying it, and makes the historian's willingness to record his country's disgrace an argument for the book's authenticity

themes: the dances and the ambush in the vineyards
the obscure plea to the fathers
